title: Why So Few People Live On Colombia's West Coast
text:

Read about this topic here: https://geographicgeoff.substack.com/

🌳 Find me elsewhere: https://linktr.ee/geographybygeoff

Colombia is an incredible country, geographically. But despite being home to over 53 million people, the second most populous country in South America, almost no one lives on the country's Pacific coast. And this is weird because most countries in the Americas have gone through great effort to settle and build population centers on their respective west coasts. So what's going on in Colombia and why have they still not developed the vast majority of their Pacific coast?

In this episode we'll cover the varied and intimidating physical geography of Colombia, how, why and where the Spanish decided to colonize and settle, and why, even into 2024, Colombia's west coast is still vastly underpopulated compared to its Andean and Caribbean regions.

title: ‘I don’t care’: Colombia’s President Petro dismisses revocation of US visa
text:
Colombian President Gustavo Petro has dismissed the decision of United States President Donald Trump’s administration to revoke his visa over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza, saying that Washington “no longer respects international law”.
“I no longer have a visa to travel to the United States. I don’t care. I don’t need a visa … because I’m not only a Colombian citizen but a European citizen, and I truly consider myself a free person in the world,” Petro wrote on X on Saturday.
The US Department of State announced in a social media post on Friday that it had stripped Petro of his US visa, citing his “reckless and incendiary actions” in relation to a speech he gave to protesters outside the United Nations headquarters in New York City.
The post did not provide specific details on Petro’s alleged offence, but footage circulated on social media earlier on Friday showed the Colombian leader joining thousands of pro-Palestine protesters outside the UN building in Midtown Manhattan.
Petro returned to Colombia on Saturday as intended, saying he found out about his visa status upon arrival.
In a post on social media, he said: ” International law grants me immunity to go to the UN and that there should be no reprisals for my free opinion, because I am a free person”.

Al Jazeera’s Alessandro Rampietti reports from Bogota, Colombia.

title: A Guide to Colombia’s Best Street Food. Travel Experiences
text:
Explore the vibrant street food scene at Plaza de la Trinidad in Getsemaní, Cartagena! Known for its lively energy, this historic square in the heart of the Getsemaní neighborhood has become one of Cartagena’s must-visit spots for locals and tourists alike. Nestled just a short walk from Cartagena’s famous Old Town, the Plaza de la Trinidad is the social heartbeat of Getsemaní. You can easily get there by walking from Old Town or taking a quick cab ride, especially if you're staying outside the walled city. Wonderful Hotels and vacation spots.

Historically, Plaza de la Trinidad has been central to Cartagena’s culture and community. The square’s namesake, the Iglesia de la Santísima Trinidad (Church of the Holy Trinity), dates back to the early 17th century. Today, the plaza serves as a gathering spot where history and modern-day culture mix. By day, it offers glimpses into local life, but it truly transforms at night when vendors set up food stalls, and the air fills with the aroma of delicious street food.

In my street food adventure, I dove into some classic dishes that define Cartagena’s nighttime food scene. First up was a juicy hamburger, stacked with all the local fixings and a unique Caribbean twist. Then came the iconic 4-meat arepa—a rich and savory delight packed with an assortment of meats, offering a taste of local flavors and an unmatched texture. For a lighter but equally satisfying bite, I tried cheese arepas—simple yet bursting with flavor. Next, I sampled picada, a mix of various grilled and fried meats often topped with chimichurri sauce, making it the ultimate Colombian comfort food. To wrap up the feast, I indulged in a sweet obleas, a thin wafer treat often filled with caramel or cheese, a popular choice among locals and tourists alike.

The Plaza de la Trinidad is more than just food; it’s a lively party atmosphere. Street performers, musicians, and dancers fill the square, creating a festive vibe that makes every visit feel like a celebration. People gather to enjoy food, dance, and the spontaneous joy that fills the air. This blend of culture, food, and nightlife is why Plaza de la Trinidad is a must-visit for anyone wanting an authentic experience of Cartagena's street food and local life.

Make sure to put Plaza de la Trinidad on your list when visiting Cartagena for an unforgettable street food experience!
